title: Address at Walla Walla, Washington
paragraphs: Mr. Mayor; and you, My Fellow Citizens; Men and Women of this beautiful garden city:

I am delighted to be with you this afternoon. (Applause) I have enjoyed thoroughly seeing your city and you. I want to say a word or two of special greeting to three or four divisions among you; first of all, of course, to the men of the Grand Army; they always come first, they have the right of the line on all occasions; (Applause) and then a word to my own comrades of the Spanish American war. All day it has done me good to see, as I have come through place after place, the liveliness of your memory of what was done in '98. It was only a skirmish compared to what you men of '61 to '65 did, but the effects were momentous upon this country and upon the world; for as the result of that struggle the United States found itself where it had to take a position of dominance on the Pacific. Here in Washington, the gateway to Alaska, with her wonderful variety of sources of wealth, with Puget Sound that absolutely unparalleled body of water, you have to take a leading part in the history of American dominance on the Pacific. You cannot help yourselves, and if I read you aright you do not want to. (Applause) Every now and then a nation like an individual finds itself where it must play a great part. All that it can decide is whether it will play that part well or ill. So it is with the United States; so it is with our great American republic. We hold a position in wealth, in numbers, in geographical location, which forces us to play a leading part in the world. We cannot help playing it; all we can decide is whether we will play it well or ill; and, my fellow countrymen, I know you too well to hesitate as to what your decision will be.

I am particularly glad to have the chance of speaking from in front of this institution of learning, an institution which commemorates the name and the great deeds of one of America's worthies, (Cheers and applause) of Whitman, who stamped his mark deep on the history of the nation. He was one of the leaders in that movement which settled that the region now making the great states of Washington and Oregon was to exist and flourish under the American flag. (Cheers and applause) I cannot sufficiently congratulate you, Mr. President, upon what has been done here with this college. I wish to pay a special tribute here in Washington to the work done by the educators in Washington. Nothing has pleased me more or impressed me more than the sedulous care given by your people to the school system, the college system, in your state. Nothing has pleased me more than to see the children and the teachers, the professors, representing the ordinary school, the high school, the normal school, the college, as I have met them coming from city to city throughout this state.

You have wonderful resources within your borders. I thought I knew pretty fairly that you had a wonderful state, and my expectations were high too, but I do not think I appreciated what a wonderful state it was. Within the half century now opening Washington will take its place as among the leading states of the Union in wealth, power, population, in all that goes to make up greatness. You have wonderful material resources. They are indispensable as a foundation, but if you build nothing upon them then you have only a foundation, and not a perfect structure. Do not misunderstand me. Every now and then I hear some one say, "You are slurring material well-being; you do not pay proper heed to the architects of industry, to the captains of industry; you do not pay proper heed to business energy, business enterprise, which must underlie business success." I do pay proper heed to them. You can no more build a great nation without them than y ou can build any building whatever without its foundation; but they only make the foundation. On them you have to build the structure of the higher life, moral, intellectual, spiritual, or else our civilization is not and will not be what it should be. (Applause) I congratulate you, my fellow citizens, upon what you are doing here in this great state in bringing up your children worthily to continue the work that the pioneers began and that you are helping carry to completion. We are a practical people, a business people, but we are infinitely more than merely a business people. If you doubt my words, do not believe them. I appeal not to what I say, but to what the men of '61 to 65 did, to what the men, your brothers and sons, did in the Philippines. You men of the civil war, when Abraham Lincoln called to arms and your hearts leaped within you did you think you were then influenced by merely business considerations? No. These men before they went to war and during the lives they have led since they came back from the war, have been good, practical, hard-working Americans; but there were four years, the best four years, of their life, that they rendered a service for Which there could be no adequate pay in gold or pecuniary reward, for they showed themselves at that time willing to lay down all, life itself, in generous fealty to a lofty ideal. (Applause) Our country is great because our people had it in them to show such loftiness of spirit when the great appeal was made to them. We never would have built this country up if it had not been for the business energy, the business enterprise, of our people; but we would have broken into fifty jangling fragments if our people had only had that business ente rprise, that business energy, when in '61 the guns of Sumter called to war.

I preach to you not only the gospel of material strife, of material endeavor to work for tangible things, but also the gospel of strife after all that is higher and nobler, the gospel of the intellectual and spiritual movement that is to make this nation not merely in material ways the greatest, but in all ways the greatest nation upon which the sun has ever shone. (Applause)

Men and women of Washington, you who have so much in soil and climate, in physical resources, upon which to pride yourselves, I hardly need remind you that after all the thing that counts most in the career of the nation is the quality of the average citizenship of that nation. No climate, no soil, no fertility, no physical resources can avail if you have not the right type of men and women, the type of man and woman which desires not pleasure merely as the end, but is glad to lead a life of worthy deeds well done. It is the quality of the average man, the average woman, that determines in the end whether a state is to go down or up. Exactly as in the civil war; the arms, the training, all else, were subordinate to the character of the man in blue. That is what was the final decisive factor. On the other hand, every man who has been in the army knows that now and then you met a man to whom you would give any weapon, any uniform, any training, and after you had done it all he was utterly worthless because if he did not have the stuff in him you could not get it out of him. (Applause) It is just so in civic life. What we need in the community is a high standard for the average man, and I do not know but an even higher standard for the average woman, because of the two in the partnership it often seems to me that the woman has a little the worst of it. I spoke of the educational movement here. The college president, the head of the school, the teachers, men and women, they are all important, but they are not all put together one-tenth as important as the mother at home. There is no type of citizen, no man, not even the man who went through the four years of the civil war, whom I think deserved quite as well of the country as many a woman whom each one of us knows, who under all kinds of adverse circumstances, yet brings up her children so that they shall not only rise up to call her blessed, but that the whole country ought to also.

One word to the under-graduates and the graduates of this college. To whom much has been given from them much is rightfully to be expected. You have received a training which does not confer upon you special privileges, because it is in itself a special privilege, but it does impose upon you certain burdens of responsibility. We have a right to expect that from the college-bred man we shall get a double service of good citizenship to the state. While I believe emphatically in play and believe in playing hard while you play, yet when you work do not play at all. We have a right to demand from you in after years the only return to the college that can be given; that is the return in honor to the college by the record you make for her in the service of the commonwealth at large. This college, this city, reminds us of the old days, the days of the pioneers, of the men who enjoyed life and yet who worked so well and so strongly. Let us, now that the pioneer days are over, endeavor to keep alive the pioneer virtues. We need just the same qualities in order to make this nation rise level to its opportunities that Whitman and his associates needed when they guided the white-topped, ox-drawn wagons across the plains, across the mountains, and settled down here to enter and possess the land, the same qualities of iron will, of forethought, of daring, of the courage that does not flinch or yield, the same power of acting each on his own responsibility, and yet of acting all in combination one with the other. The old pioneer days have gone, the days when the pioneers rendered, and when side by side with them those men whom all good Americans delight to honor-- the officers and enlisted men of the regular army-- rendered inestimable service at infinite cost to themsel ves. Those days have gone, but new problems ever loom before us from within and from without. The immense and complex industrial development of our nation within, the constant increase in the commanding position it assumes abroad, all demand on our part every ounce of courage, of capacity for work and capacity for sane judgment which we have. Many problems arise for solution before us. The details of that solution differ infinitely from one generation to another, but the spirit in which they are to be approached remains unchanged. We must approach them in the spirit of the men who under Washington founded the republic, of the men who under Lincoln saved the republic. We must show the qualities they showed. Those qualities are not especially genius, not especially brilliancy, but the old, hundrum, work-a-day qualities which in the aggregate have made all really great and masterful races from the earliest day of which recorded history tells us. Unless we have as a people self-mastery and self-restraint, joined with that the power to do, to dare, to endure, to aspire, and finally the power to do it all in sane and sober fashion; unless we have that power we will not succeed.. [?] And we shall succeed; we shall build up this republic to a greatness of which even we now in our fondest dreams do not think, because the average American has it in him, and I firmly believe will transmit to his children and to his children's children, exactly the type of characteristic which enabled us to make out of thirteen little colonies on the Atlantic seaboard the germ of the mighty continental nation which now grasps an ocean in either hand. We shall succeed because we have in us the qualities that made the union armies in the civil war finally triumph. As a nation we need and shall have strong bodies; we need and shall have strong minds, and then we need and have what is greater than body, greater than mind -- character; character, into which many elements enter, but three above all.-- In the first place as the ground work, decency, honesty, clean living, high thinking, fair dealing as between man and man, and in addition thereto the qualities of which we speak when we say of a man that he is not only a good man but emphatically a man, the qualities of courage, of strength, of hardihood, the qualities that give a man will power, and energy, and resourcefulness, and self-reliance; and in addition to honesty and to courage as a nation we have and will keep the third quality, the quality needed to guide and moderate both the others -- the saving grace of common sense. (Cheers and applause)

Unless we have as a people self-mastery and self-restraint, jpined with that the power to do, to dare, to endure, to aspire, and finally the power to do it all in sane and sober fashion; unless we have that power we wouldwill not succeed. . And we shall succeed; we shall build up this republic to a greatness of which even we now in our fondest dreams do not think, because the average American has it in him, and I firmly believe will transmit to his children and to his children's children, exactly the type of characteristic which enabled us to make out of thirteen little colonies on the Atlantic seaboard the germ of the mighty continental nation which now grasps an ocean in either hand. We shall succeed because we have in us the qualities that made the union armies in the civil war finally triumph. As a nation we need and shall have strong bodies; we need and shall have strong minds, and then we need and have what is greater than body, gre ater than mind -- character; character, into which many elements enter, but three above all.-- In the first place as the ground work, decency, honesty, clean living, high thinking, fair dealing as between man and man, and in addition thereto the qualities of which we speak when we say of a man that he is not only a good man but emphatically a man, the qualities of courage, of strength, of hardihood, the qualities that give a man will power, and energy, and resourcefulness, and self-reliance; and in addition to honesty and to courage as a nation we have and will keep the third quality, the quality needed to guide and moderate both the others -- the saving grace of common sense. (Cheers and applause)
